slides.say: A cyclist rides from home to work at a constant speed. If she rode twenty-five percent faster, the trip would take twelve minutes less. How many minutes does the trip take at her usual speed?
at: A cyclist rides from home to work

slides.say: So the route is the same, and the speed changes by a percent. They ask for the usual time, not the new one.
at: They ask for the usual time

slides.say: We'll solve it in two different ways. First by understanding, like in the lesson. Twenty-five percent faster is times five quarters. On the same route we flip it, so the time is times four fifths.
at: so the time is times four fifths

slides.say: Times four fifths means one fifth of the trip is saved. And the question says the saving is twelve minutes.
at: one fifth of the trip is saved

slides.say: So one fifth of the trip is twelve minutes. The whole trip is five times twelve, sixty minutes.
Careful with forty-eight, choice number two. It's sixty minus twelve, the new time. And it's also what you get if you think the time drops by twenty-five percent. They ask for the usual time.
at: They ask for the usual time

slides.say: [pause] Now let's plug in the answers. We start again from the givens. Let's try sixty minutes. To make it easy, say the trip is sixty kilometers at sixty kilometers per hour. That takes one hour, sixty minutes.
Now she rides twenty-five percent faster. A quarter of sixty is fifteen, so sixty plus fifteen, seventy-five kilometers per hour.
Sixty kilometers at seventy-five is sixty over seventy-five, four fifths of an hour. That's forty-eight minutes.
Sixty minus forty-eight is twelve minutes less. That's exactly the given.
Choice number three is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number three is our answer
